subsections.subsection_title: What the OSCE station may say

blocks.text: A hysterosalpingogram (HSG) is a fluoroscopic contrast study used primarily to evaluate the uterine cavity and fallopian tube patency during the investigation of infertility.
Representative HSG images: the uterine cavity fills with contrast, both tubes opacify, and contrast spills freely into the peritoneal cavity when the tubes are patent.
A 30-year-old woman with primary infertility undergoes HSG. The uterine cavity has a normal triangular outline, both fallopian tubes fill with contrast, and there is bilateral free peritoneal spill.
Tasks: Describe the image, interpret the findings and explain their significance.
A 32-year-old woman with a history of pelvic inflammatory disease has an HSG showing a normally outlined uterine cavity but failure of contrast to pass beyond the proximal portions of both tubes.
Tasks: Identify the abnormality, give possible causes, discuss potential artefacts and outline further management.
A 34-year-old woman with infertility has an HSG showing a dilated, tortuous fallopian tube with distal obstruction and no free peritoneal spill.
Tasks: Interpret the image, explain the pathophysiology and discuss fertility implications.
A 27-year-old woman with recurrent pregnancy loss has an HSG demonstrating an abnormal uterine cavity contour.
Tasks: Describe the abnormality, differentiate congenital uterine anomalies from acquired lesions, and recommend further investigations.
Recognition of normal uterine and tubal anatomy.
Identification of tubal patency or obstruction.
Recognition of uterine cavity abnormalities.
Awareness of technical pitfalls and false-positive obstruction.
Appropriate differential diagnoses and infertility management.
In a pure image-interpretation station, you do not need to perform the procedure. If asked to counsel a patient before HSG, use a structured approach.

“Hysterosalpingography is an X-ray procedure in which contrast material is introduced through the cervix into the uterus. Images are then taken to assess the shape of the uterine cavity and whether the fallopian tubes are open. This can help identify some causes of infertility. I would explain the benefits, risks, alternatives and timing of the procedure before obtaining your consent.”
Before HSG, establish:
The indication, including infertility or selected uterine cavity concerns.
The first day of the last menstrual period and cycle regularity.
Whether pregnancy is possible.
Any current pelvic pain, fever or abnormal vaginal discharge.
Previous pelvic inflammatory disease or sexually transmitted infection.
Previous reactions to iodinated contrast.
Relevant allergies and medical history.
Previous uterine or tubal surgery.
Do not perform routine HSG in:
Known or suspected pregnancy.
Active pelvic inflammatory disease.
Active significant genital tract infection.
Significant unexplained bleeding where assessment is required before proceeding.
HSG is commonly scheduled after menstruation and before ovulation, often around cycle days 7–10 in a regular cycle, according to local protocol.
Antibiotic prophylaxis is not required for every patient but may be considered for selected patients, particularly those with previous pelvic infection or hydrosalpinx, according to local guidance.
Examiner tip: HSG uses ionising radiation and iodinated contrast. Check pregnancy status, infection risk and previous contrast reactions before proceeding.
Fluoroscopy machine.
Radiolucent examination table.
Vaginal speculum.
Antiseptic solution.
Sterile gloves and drapes.
HSG catheter or cannula.
Syringe containing water-soluble iodinated contrast.
Appropriate emergency equipment for contrast reactions.
The patient is usually positioned supine in the lithotomy position.
Explain each step and confirm consent.
Perform a pregnancy and infection safety check.
Ensure privacy and appropriate chaperoning.
Insert a speculum to visualise the cervix.
Clean the cervix using an appropriate antiseptic.
Insert the HSG catheter or cannula through the cervical canal.
Slowly introduce contrast under fluoroscopic guidance.
Obtain images of the uterine cavity, fallopian tubes and peritoneal spill.
Remove the catheter and assess the patient before discharge.
Uterine cavity shape and filling defects.
Whether each tube fills.
The location of any suspected obstruction.
Presence or absence of free peritoneal spill on each side.
Any tubal dilatation or loculated spill.
Technical limitations or patient intolerance.

HSG is a relatively brief procedure, but cramping, spotting and temporary discomfort can occur. The patient should receive instructions on when to seek care for fever, worsening pelvic pain or foul-smelling discharge.
Use the mnemonic C-A-T-S.
Assess the uterine outline, size, symmetry and contour. Look for filling defects, adhesions and congenital abnormalities.
Follow the right and left tubes from the uterine cornua through the isthmic and ampullary portions towards the fimbrial ends.
Determine whether contrast traverses each tube and whether it spills freely into the peritoneal cavity.
Look for free or loculated spill, hydrosalpinx, peritubal adhesions and possible technical artefacts.
The normal contrast pattern consists of:
A smooth, approximately triangular uterine cavity.
Symmetrical uterine cornua.
Opacification of both fallopian tubes.
No persistent filling defects.
Free spill of contrast from both fimbrial ends into the peritoneal cavity.
Key distinction: A tube that fills with contrast is not necessarily patent throughout. The strongest evidence of patency is contrast passing through the tube with free peritoneal spill.
Normal triangular configuration.
Smooth outline.
No obvious filling defects.
No evidence of significant cavity distortion.
Both tubes are visualised.
Normal calibre and contour.
No obvious dilatation.
Free bilateral peritoneal spill.

“This is a hysterosalpingogram demonstrating a normally outlined triangular uterine cavity with no obvious filling defects. Both fallopian tubes are visualised and demonstrate contrast passage with free bilateral peritoneal spill. These findings indicate bilateral tubal patency, with no obvious uterine cavity abnormality on this study.”

content_groups.group_title: What does a normal HSG mean?

blocks.text: It supports the conclusion that:
Both tubes are patent at the time of examination.
There is no major radiographically visible cavity defect.
There is no obvious complete tubal obstruction.
However, a normal HSG does not exclude endometriosis, peritubal adhesions, subtle tubal dysfunction, ovulatory disorders, male-factor infertility or all forms of uterine pathology.
The uterine cavity fills normally.
Contrast reaches the uterine cornua.
Both tubes fail to opacify beyond their proximal segments.
No free peritoneal spill is demonstrated.
Bilateral proximal tubal occlusion is suspected.
Transient cornual spasm.
Mucus or debris obstructing the proximal tubes.
Proximal tubal scarring after infection.
Previous tubal surgery or sterilisation.
Technical difficulty, including catheter position or inadequate contrast pressure.

“The uterine cavity is normally outlined. There is failure of contrast opacification beyond the proximal portions of both fallopian tubes, with no demonstrable peritoneal spill. The findings are suspicious for bilateral proximal tubal occlusion. However, transient tubal spasm or technical factors should be excluded before confirming true obstruction.”
Review the images and technical adequacy.
Consider repeat HSG or hysterosalpingo-contrast sonography where appropriate.
Consider selective salpingography with tubal cannulation in suitable patients.
Assess other infertility factors concurrently.
Refer for fertility specialist evaluation if bilateral obstruction is confirmed.
Examiner pearl: Never diagnose irreversible bilateral tubal damage from an equivocal HSG alone. Apparent proximal occlusion is particularly prone to false-positive results.
The uterine cavity is normal.
One tube fills and spills freely.
The other tube fails to opacify beyond its proximal segment.

“The uterine cavity is normal. The right fallopian tube demonstrates contrast passage and free peritoneal spill. The left tube fails to opacify beyond its proximal portion, raising suspicion of left proximal tubal obstruction. Correlation with the technical quality of the study is recommended.”
Natural conception may still occur with one patent, functional tube, depending on other fertility factors. However, the HSG does not establish normal tubal function or guarantee fertility.
Consider expectant management when clinically appropriate.
Investigate ovulation, ovarian reserve where indicated and semen parameters.
Further assess suspected obstruction if it would change management.
Consider selective tubal cannulation for confirmed proximal obstruction in appropriately selected patients.
Discuss assisted reproduction when indicated by the complete fertility assessment.

content_groups.group_title: Case 3 — Distal tubal obstruction with hydrosalpinx

blocks.text: The tube fills with contrast.
The distal tube is dilated and tortuous.
Contrast does not spill freely from the fimbrial end.
A club-shaped or elongated contrast-filled tube may be visible.
A hydrosalpinx is a dilated fallopian tube filled with fluid, usually resulting from distal tubal obstruction and chronic inflammatory damage.
Previous pelvic inflammatory disease.
Previous sexually transmitted infection, including chlamydial infection.
Endometriosis.
Previous pelvic or tubal surgery.
Adhesive disease.

“The HSG demonstrates a dilated, tortuous fallopian tube with distal obstruction and no free peritoneal spill, consistent with hydrosalpinx. The contralateral tube should be assessed separately for patency and morphology.”
It may impair fertility through tubal dysfunction and is associated with poorer IVF outcomes when communicating with the uterine cavity.
Refer to a fertility specialist.
Assess the contralateral tube and other infertility factors.
Discuss surgical options in selected patients.
Consider salpingectomy or proximal tubal occlusion before IVF in appropriately selected patients with hydrosalpinx.
Individualise treatment according to age, ovarian reserve, tubal anatomy and fertility goals.
ASRM guidance discusses tubal cannulation for selected proximal obstruction and treatment of surgically irreparable hydrosalpinx before IVF.

content_groups.group_title: Case 4 — Peritubal adhesions and loculated spill

blocks.text: Contrast passes through the tube.
Spill occurs, but it pools in a confined or irregular distribution.
Contrast may appear trapped around the adnexa rather than dispersing freely.
The tube may be angulated or appear tethered.
These findings raise suspicion of peritubal adhesions, which can occur following pelvic infection, endometriosis or previous surgery.

“Both fallopian tubes demonstrate contrast opacification. There is loculated peritoneal spill adjacent to the right adnexa, raising suspicion of right peritubal adhesions. The findings should be correlated with the clinical history and other investigations.”
Peritubal adhesions.
Loculated contrast due to pelvic inflammatory disease.
Endometriosis-related adhesions.
Technical or projection-related appearances.
Assess other infertility factors.
Consider specialist pelvic ultrasound or other imaging where appropriate.
Consider laparoscopy with chromopertubation if surgery is indicated for a separate clinical reason or if the findings would materially alter management.

Important: HSG may suggest adhesions but cannot reliably map all external pelvic adhesions. Laparoscopy allows direct visualisation, although it is not recommended routinely for every infertility investigation.

content_groups.group_title: Case 5 — Uterine cavity filling defect: endometrial polyp

blocks.text: A smooth, rounded or oval filling defect.
Contrast outlines the defect.
The rest of the uterine cavity may appear normal.
Tubal patency may be normal or abnormal independently.
Endometrial polyp.
Submucosal fibroid.
Intrauterine adhesions.
Blood clot or air bubble.
Less commonly, another endometrial lesion.

“The uterine cavity demonstrates a smooth, rounded filling defect along the fundal region, suspicious for an endometrial polyp. Both fallopian tubes should be assessed independently for patency. Further assessment of the cavity is recommended.”
Transvaginal ultrasound.
Saline infusion sonography.
Hysteroscopy, which allows direct visualisation and possible removal.
Histopathological assessment when tissue is removed or sampling is indicated.

Management depends on symptoms, lesion size, fertility plans and the risk of significant pathology. Hysteroscopic polypectomy may be appropriate for symptomatic patients or selected patients undergoing fertility evaluation.
A smooth or lobulated filling defect.
Distortion or indentation of the uterine cavity.
The lesion may be broad-based.
Tubes may remain patent.

“There is a smooth filling defect arising from the uterine cavity wall, producing focal distortion of the cavity contour. The appearance raises suspicion of a submucosal leiomyoma. Transvaginal ultrasound, saline infusion sonography or hysteroscopy may help characterise the lesion.”
An endometrial polyp can also produce a filling defect. HSG alone may not reliably distinguish a polyp from a submucosal fibroid.
If the lesion causes relevant symptoms, distorts the cavity or is considered significant in the patient's fertility assessment, hysteroscopic myomectomy may be considered.
Irregular, angular or linear filling defects.
Partial obliteration of the uterine cavity.
Distortion of the cavity shape.
Reduced cavity capacity in severe disease.
Previous uterine evacuation or curettage.
History of retained products of conception.
Previous intrauterine surgery.
Hypomenorrhoea or amenorrhoea.
Infertility or recurrent pregnancy loss.

“The uterine cavity demonstrates multiple irregular filling defects and partial obliteration, suspicious for intrauterine adhesions. The clinical history of previous uterine instrumentation supports this possibility. Hysteroscopy is recommended for definitive assessment and possible treatment.”
Hysteroscopy to confirm the diagnosis.
Hysteroscopic adhesiolysis when appropriate.
Follow-up assessment for recurrence.
Individualised reproductive counselling.
Examiner pearl: HSG can suggest intrauterine adhesions, but hysteroscopy provides direct visualisation and is particularly useful when treatment is planned.
The uterine cavity may appear divided by a central filling defect, creating two upper cavity channels.
The upper uterine cavity is divided into two horns, often with a deep external fundal cleft.
A single, narrow, asymmetric uterine cavity may be visualised.
Two separate uterine cavities may be present. HSG may demonstrate the cavities separately, but the external uterine anatomy is not adequately characterised by HSG alone.

“The HSG demonstrates an abnormal uterine cavity configuration with division of the upper cavity into two channels. A congenital Müllerian anomaly is suspected. Three-dimensional transvaginal ultrasound or MRI is recommended to assess the external fundal contour and distinguish a septate from a bicornuate uterus.”
A septate uterus and a bicornuate uterus have different anatomical features and may require different management. HSG demonstrates the cavity but does not reliably define the external fundal contour.
Examiner tip: Do not diagnose a bicornuate uterus solely because the cavity looks divided on HSG. Correlate with three-dimensional ultrasound or MRI.
Multiple small diverticular contrast-filled outpouchings along the isthmic portion of a fallopian tube.
Nodular or irregular tubal contour.
Possible associated tubal obstruction.

“The HSG demonstrates multiple small contrast-filled diverticular outpouchings along the isthmic portion of the fallopian tube, consistent with salpingitis isthmica nodosa. This abnormality may be associated with tubal-factor infertility and ectopic pregnancy.”
Fertility specialist assessment.
Evaluate the severity and distribution of tubal disease.
Discuss appropriate fertility options, including assisted reproduction when indicated.

content_groups.group_title: Case 10 — Tubal ligation or previous tubal surgery

blocks.text: Contrast fills the uterine cavity.
Tubal opacification may terminate at the expected site of occlusion.
No spill occurs beyond the occluded segments.
Surgical clips may or may not be visible, depending on the procedure and image.
“The uterine cavity is normally outlined. There is no contrast passage beyond the expected sites of tubal occlusion, consistent with previous tubal sterilisation in the appropriate clinical context.”

content_groups.group_title: Examiner question: Can HSG be used to investigate previous tubal ligation?

blocks.text: Yes, in selected situations. HSG may be used to assess tubal occlusion after certain sterilisation procedures or investigate suspected tubal patency, depending on the procedure performed.
Intravasation occurs when contrast enters uterine or pelvic blood vessels rather than remaining within the uterine cavity and fallopian tubes.
Fine, branching vascular channels become opacified.
Contrast may rapidly track away from the uterine cavity.
The pattern may resemble vessels rather than free peritoneal spill.
Excessive injection pressure.
Recent pregnancy or uterine instrumentation.
Increased intrauterine pressure.
Conditions that may compromise the endometrial–myometrial interface.

“There is evidence of contrast intravasation, with opacification of branching vascular channels adjacent to the uterus. The appearance should not be mistaken for normal tubal spill. The procedure should be reviewed by the performing clinician, and further contrast injection should be avoided if safety is in question.”

content_groups.group_title: Case 12 — Apparent tubal obstruction due to technical factors

blocks.text: Cornual spasm.
Catheter displacement.
Contrast leakage through the cervix.
Inadequate contrast filling.
Patient movement.
Inadequate imaging of delayed spill.

“The study is technically limited by inadequate opacification of the proximal tubes and contrast leakage. Tubal patency cannot be reliably determined from these images. Repeat or alternative assessment should be considered if clinically indicated.”
Examiner pearl: A technically inadequate HSG is not the same as a diagnostic HSG showing tubal obstruction.
Use the following format in an image interpretation station.
Examination: Hysterosalpingography.
Uterine cavity: Describe shape, size, symmetry, contour and filling defects.
Right fallopian tube: Describe opacification, calibre, course, suspected obstruction and peritoneal spill.
Left fallopian tube: Describe opacification, calibre, course, suspected obstruction and peritoneal spill.
Additional findings: Hydrosalpinx, loculated spill, intravasation or technical limitations.
Impression: State the most likely diagnosis and whether the tubes appear patent.
Recommendation: Suggest further assessment only where clinically indicated.

blocks.text: HSG is an important first-line investigation of tubal patency, but abnormal results sometimes require confirmation.
Do not investigate only the female reproductive tract.
Assess:
Ovulation and menstrual history.
Semen parameters.
Uterine anatomy.
Tubal patency.
Age and duration of infertility.
Previous pregnancies, ectopic pregnancy and pelvic infection.
Relevant ovarian reserve testing where it will guide treatment.
Management is based on the underlying pathology, the patient's reproductive goals and the complete fertility assessment.

blocks.text: Exclude spasm; consider selective tubal cannulation where appropriate.
Assess tubal damage and discuss surgery versus assisted reproduction.
Characterise with ultrasound or hysteroscopy and treat if indicated.
Clarify anatomy with 3D ultrasound or MRI and individualise management.
Integrate tubal findings with age, ovarian function, semen analysis and fertility preferences.
Proximal obstruction: selected patients may benefit from tubal cannulation.
Hydrosalpinx: selected patients proceeding to IVF may benefit from salpingectomy or proximal tubal occlusion.
Intrauterine adhesions: hysteroscopic treatment may be appropriate.
Submucosal fibroids or polyps: consider hysteroscopic treatment where clinically indicated.
Congenital uterine anomalies: confirm the specific anomaly before considering corrective treatment.
Bilateral severe tubal disease: discuss IVF and other fertility options.
Active infection: treat the infection; do not proceed with routine HSG during active pelvic infection.
The choice between tubal surgery and IVF depends on factors including the site and severity of disease, age, ovarian reserve, other infertility factors and patient preference.

subsections.subsection_title: Final examiner-ready summary and practice station

blocks.text: “This is a hysterosalpingogram performed to assess the uterine cavity and fallopian tube patency. I would first assess the shape and contour of the uterine cavity and look for filling defects. I would then follow each fallopian tube from its uterine insertion to its distal end, describing the calibre, course and any suspected obstruction. Finally, I would assess whether contrast spills freely into the peritoneal cavity on each side and look for hydrosalpinx, loculated spill or technical limitations. I would summarise the findings, give the most likely diagnosis and recommend further investigations or fertility specialist assessment where appropriate.”
1. An HSG shows a normal uterine cavity, bilateral tubal opacification and free spill from both tubes. What is the interpretation?
2. Contrast stops abruptly at both uterine cornua. What should you consider before diagnosing bilateral obstruction?

items: B. Cornual spasm or technical artefact

blocks.text: 3. A fallopian tube is dilated, tortuous and has no distal spill. What is the most likely diagnosis?
4. HSG shows irregular linear filling defects and partial obliteration of the uterine cavity in a woman with previous curettage. What is the likely diagnosis?
5. HSG suggests a divided uterine cavity. Which investigation best helps distinguish a septate from a bicornuate uterus?

items: D. Three-dimensional transvaginal ultrasound or MRI
